path: September: Moody outspends a low-profile Democrat; national Democrats invest little in Florida. Deportation and TPS controversies get South Florida coverage, but Moody keeps clear of the issue.

October: Polls show Hispanic softening in Miami-Dade, but the Democrat cannot afford a large Spanish-language ad campaign. Republican turnout operations stay strong while the national environment leans Democratic.
November 3: Miami-Dade swings back toward Democrats from Trump's 11-point win but stays narrowly Republican. Moody wins statewide comfortably.
September: The Democratic nominee unites the party after the primary. Rogers courts union and working-class voters in Flint with tariff and auto messaging.
October: The national environment favors Democrats; unions and Black churches in Flint mobilize. Auto-sector worries hurt Republicans more than Democrats.
November 3: The Democrat carries Genesee by a mid-single-digit margin, better than Harris and Slotkin did, as the midterm swing outweighs lower turnout.
September: The Democratic nominee builds a big Oakland base on suburban fundraising. Rogers works to limit losses among college graduates.
October: Anti-incumbent suburban sentiment deepens. No scandal hits the Democrat.
November 3: The Democrat wins Oakland by double digits.
September: The Republican primary winner tries to consolidate the party. Talarico or Crockett draws national money, and Tarrant becomes a target county for both sides.
October: The midterm backlash and Hispanic movement back toward Democrats narrow the gap. Suburban moderates are split, and Paxton's scandals cost Republicans some ticket-splitters.
November 3: Tarrant is very close. The Republican edges it in most scenarios, but a Democratic wave flips it.
September: The Republican nominee leans on Collin's party infrastructure. The Democrat campaigns in the affluent suburbs.
October: Suburban anti-Trump sentiment grows, but the county's Republican base holds. Some traditional Republicans split their tickets if Paxton is the nominee.
November 3: Collin narrows to a margin of a few points but stays Republican.
September: Lombardo runs on his vetoes and independence from Trump. Ford tries to nationalize the race.
October: Washoe moderates and nonpartisans split their tickets. The national environment helps Ford, but Lombardo keeps a personal brand advantage in the north.
November: Washoe is close. Lombardo's incumbency usually carries it narrowly, though a Democratic wave could tip it to Ford.
September: Hobbs faces Biggs, or another Republican nominee, and portrays him as extreme. Her large war chest funds suburban ads in Maricopa.
October: The midterm environment favors the out-party, Democrats. Independents and moderate Republicans in the suburbs lean toward Hobbs.
November: Counting in Maricopa is slow, but Hobbs leads it by a few points. Results are known by November 7 or soon after.
Early September: The Kremlin finalizes registrations. The Greens run a party list polling around 1% and a few district candidates.
September 18-20: United Russia stands aside in a few districts for allies, mostly Rodina, Party of Growth and similar parties. The Greens are not clearly favored.
Results: The Greens get about 1% on the list and probably no district seat, unless the Kremlin gave them a deal.
Early September: LDPR campaigns as the leading opposition party under Slutsky. The Kremlin manages turnout and the vote count.
September 18-20: LDPR improves on its 2021 result and may finish second on the list. United Russia keeps most districts.
Results: LDPR wins roughly 30-60 seats, far short of 95.
Early September: New People campaigns among urban and younger voters. The Kremlin keeps it in a safety-valve role.
September 18-20: New People clears 5% again with about 6-8% of the list vote and wins few or no districts.
Results: New People wins roughly 15-28 seats, under 35.
September: Witkoff and Kushner shuttle between the sides. Fighting continues, and both sides keep saying they are open to talks.
October: With the US pushing for a win before the midterms, a trilateral round is convened in the Gulf or in Geneva. Delegations or mediated in-person contacts take place.
Through November 10: At least one in-person meeting, direct or mediated, discusses ceasefire terms, unless an escalation freezes the process.
September 2-10: The blockade stays in place as leverage. Iran resists talks under pressure, and Oman and Qatar quietly mediate.
September 10-20: No interim deal emerges. Beijing complains, but no date for a Xi visit is close.
By September 24: There is no official announcement lifting or suspending the blockade.
September: Young men's disapproval of Trump grows over prices. Democrats push podcast and online outreach.
October: Republicans lack Trump on the ballot, and turnout among low-propensity young men drops. The national environment leans Democratic.
November 3: The CNN exit poll, likely the 18-29 men crosstab, shows Democrats narrowly ahead or about even. Republicans win it in a minority of scenarios.
September: Deportation raids and costs keep Latino men drifting back toward Democrats, and Democrats campaign on enforcement excesses.
October: The swing back seen in 2025 holds, and Republicans lack Trump on the ballot.
November 3: The CNN exit poll shows Democrats winning Latino men, by less than in 2018 but clearly ahead.
September 3-15: Trump publicly backs Hegseth amid continuing criticism. No new major scandal appears.
September 15-25: Republicans avoid any shake-up before the midterms, and Hegseth shows no sign of leaving.
By September 30: Hegseth is still in office.
September: Hegseth keeps Trump's backing despite controversies.
October: The midterm campaign discourages a reshuffle, and any new scandal is absorbed rather than acted on.
By October 31: Hegseth is still in office. Any change is likelier after the election.
September: Nominations close. Jarman recontests on Devonport's Living City record, and one or two councillors challenge her.
October: Postal voting proceeds. Name recognition favors the incumbent, and local rate concerns are moderate.
October 27-28: Jarman is re-elected in most scenarios, unless she retired or a strong challenger emerged.
September: Fuller probably recontests, and a councillor or the deputy mayor may challenge her.
October: Postal voting runs on rates and services, and incumbency gives her a profile advantage.
October 27-28: Fuller is re-elected more often than not. Her retirement or a strong challenger are the main risks.
September: Doyle recontests after her first term. Huon Valley's history of council tensions produces challengers.
October: Postal voting focuses on planning and growth, and a fragmented field helps the incumbent.
October 27-29: Doyle wins narrowly in the typical case.
September: Nominations close, and it becomes clear whether long-serving Freshney runs again. Age makes retirement plausible.
October: If he runs, his personal familiarity dominates in a small electorate.
October 27-29: Freshney is re-elected if he stood. A retirement resolves this No.
September: Santos campaigns online and pressures broadcasters, including legally, for invitations. Major campaigns resist adding him.
Mid-to-late September: Smaller outlets or one major broadcaster weigh discretionary invitations, and Santos's polling in low single digits is a hurdle.
By October 3: He likely gets into at least one televised debate, such as an online-TV hybrid, but exclusion remains plausible.
September: The Together list campaigns as the main anti-Netanyahu vehicle. Likud attacks the merger, and Eisenkot and others compete for the same voters.
October: Polls put the combined list around 18-26 seats. Security events shift votes, and there is some chance of further mergers.
October 27 results: Together lands somewhere around 20-24 seats in the central case. The 17-19 bracket is one of several plausible outcomes.
September: Democrats campaign on abortion and costs, while Republicans rely on non-college white women.
October: The midterm environment leans Democratic and women swing toward Democrats, but the education divide limits the shift.
November 3: The CNN exit poll shows white women roughly even. A tie favors Democrats alphabetically, so Republicans need a clear edge.
Early September: Broistedt runs on incumbency. Dinger is one of several challengers with an unclear profile.
September 13: No one wins a majority, so a runoff is likely. The question is whether Dinger reaches it.
September 27: The incumbent or an SPD-backed rival is more likely to win than Dinger.
September: Mayes campaigns on her litigation against Trump. Petersen leans on the Republican registration edge.
October: The midterm environment with a Republican president helps Democrats, and Mayes's incumbency profile outweighs her ethics criticism.
November: Mayes wins a close race in most scenarios. Counting takes days.
September: Uthmeier runs with DeSantis's backing. The Democrat is under-funded.
October: The Hope Florida issue gets some coverage but does not escalate. Florida's Republican advantage holds.
November 3: Uthmeier wins comfortably even with the margin narrowed.
September: Republicans attack Ellison on fraud oversight, and Ellison runs on suing the Trump administration.
October: The DFL-leaning state and midterm environment help Ellison. The fraud-scandal attacks stay partly effective.
November 3: Ellison wins by a few points.
September: James campaigns as a Trump antagonist against a little-known Republican.
October: There is no re-indictment, or it backfires, and Democratic turnout holds.
November 3: James wins comfortably.
September: The Republican convention nominee runs on Indiana's partisan lean despite Morales's controversies.
October: The Democrat gets little traction, and the midterm swing is not enough.
November 3: The Republican wins by a double-digit margin.
September: Patrick outspends a low-profile Democrat.
October: Hispanic voters move somewhat back toward Democrats, but Republican structural strength holds.
November 3: Patrick wins by mid-to-high single digits.
